one_liner: LLVM's drop-in linker (ELF, COFF, Mach-O, Wasm): roughly 2x to 12x faster than GNU ld and gold, though mold and wild now beat it.
what_it_does: lld is the LLVM project's linker, installed as ld.lld (ELF), lld-link (Windows PE/COFF), ld64.lld (Mach-O) and wasm-ld. Each port is a native linker for its format. On ELF it takes the same command line and linker scripts as GNU ld and is selected with -fuse-ld=lld or by symlinking it over /usr/bin/ld. It can also be embedded as a library through lld::lldMain, and it always cross-links: every target is built in, so no per-target build is needed.
how_it_is_fast: The design document (NewLLD.md) puts it as doing less work: section contents and relocations are not read until they are needed, and each symbol name is hashed into the symbol table only once. After that the linker works through Symbol pointers that resolution replaces in place, using placement new. Archives are handled the Windows way: lld remembers every archive symbol it has seen, so it never rescans archives or loops over --start-group. Input loading, post-parse, ICF, the sharded string merging in MergeNoTailSection (32 shards keyed by high hash bits), .gdb_index construction and output writing all run on LLVM's parallelFor. The 2017 docs table shows most of the gain comes from doing less work rather than from threads: single-threaded lld beats single-threaded gold 1.9x to 2.8x, and 40 threads add only 1.7x to 2.8x more.
when_to_use: Replacing GNU ld (BFD) for large C, C++ or Rust ELF links. On a Ryzen 9 9955HX, lld 21.1.8 linked ripgrep 4.9x, wild-debug 7.0x and mold-gdb-index 12.1x faster than GNU ld 2.46 (derived from page data).
Replacing GNU gold, which binutils 2.44 (Feb 2025) deprecated and moved out of the default tarball. lld also beat gold 2.9x to 4.4x on threaded debug links in its own 2017 table.
Toolchains that already ship lld. rustc uses rust-lld by default on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu since 1.90.0, where the Rust team measured 7x faster linking for an incremental ripgrep debug rebuild.

Cross-compiling or targeting several object formats with one linker: ELF for AArch64, ARM, LoongArch, PPC/PPC64, RISC-V, x86 and x86-64 at 'production quality', plus PE/COFF with PDB debug info, Mach-O and WebAssembly.
Clang LTO and ThinLTO without a linker plugin, since bitcode is read natively; or embedding the linker in a tool through lld::lldMain.
when_not_to_use: When link time on ELF is the bottleneck and mold or wild can link your program. On Wild's page lld is 6.2s vs 2.06s for mold and 0.99s for wild on chrome, and 7.7s vs 3.6s and 2.5s on clang-debug. mold's August 2026 table has lld 3.8x to 16.1x slower than mold on a Threadripper 7980X.

Expecting gains from many-core machines: unless --threads= is given, lld caps itself at 16 threads. Its own commit a8788de1 reports that more than 16 threads made links slower, so extra cores do not help it.

Tiny links or linker-plugin LTO, where gains mostly vanish: c-hello-world was 1.06x faster than GNU ld, and in wild-lto lld (11.4s) is within 8% of GNU ld, mold and wild because LLVM code generation dominates.

Builds that depend on GNU ld's exact archive-order semantics or on undocumented linker-script corner cases. Rust's announcement warns that lld 'is not bug-for-bug compatible with GNU ld', and ELF/linker_script.md lists intentional deviations.

Small-memory build machines when moving from GNU ld: on ripgrep lld's peak RSS was 177 MiB vs 95 MiB for GNU ld (read from Wild's chart). On the big links it uses less memory than mold, for example 9.1 GiB vs 9.5 GiB on chrome.

integration.form: Built from the llvm-project monorepo. Ships as a CLI binary (lld, with symlinks ld.lld, lld-link, ld64.lld and wasm-ld) and as static driver libraries (lldELF, lldCOFF, lldMachO, lldWasm, lldMinGW) for embedding through lld::lldMain.
integration.dependencies: LLVM core libraries from the same tree (Support, Object, LTO and the target backends); CMake >= 3.20 and Python >= 3.8 to build; zlib or zstd optional for compressed debug sections.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (LLVM_REQUIRED_CXX_STANDARD 17); host compiler Clang 5.0, Apple Clang 10.0, GCC 7.4 or Visual Studio 2019 16.8 or newer.
integration.platforms: Runs wherever LLVM builds: Linux, BSDs, macOS, Windows. Targets ELF (AArch64, ARM >= v4, LoongArch, PowerPC, PowerPC64, RISC-V, x86-32 and x86-64 at production quality; MIPS 'decent'; also AMDGPU, Hexagon and SPARC V9), PE/COFF (complete, including PDB), Mach-O and WebAssembly, listed by the docs in descending order of completeness.
integration.thread_safety: As a CLI it is internally multithreaded via LLVM's parallel strategy (capped at 16 threads unless --threads=N; --threads=1 disables threading). As a library, Driver.h describes lldMain as 'safe for re-entry' with crash recovery, and its canRunAgain flag reports whether another call is safe. Running several links concurrently in one process is not documented. Open issue #66974: exitLld called from a worker thread races in llvm_shutdown.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it accepts GNU ld/gold command lines and linker scripts and is selected with -fuse-ld=lld, but archive resolution differs on purpose: --start-group is redundant, and a link can succeed under lld that fails under GNU ld or pick a different archive member. Linker-script behaviour also deviates in documented corner cases.

gotchas: Undocumented thread cap: Driver.cpp limits lld to 16 threads when --threads= is not given, but the --threads help text in Options.td still says 'By default all available hardware threads are used'. Every third-party comparison run at default options (Wild's runner passes no thread flag; mold's README says 'default options' on a 64-core Threadripper) measures lld at 16 threads, which its maintainers say is its best setting.

Archive semantics: lld remembers the symbol tables of archives it has already passed, so 'ld def.a ref.o' links under lld but fails under GNU ld. When two archives define the same symbol, the two linkers can silently pick different objects. Use --warn-backrefs to find these cases before switching.

The headline docs table cannot be rerun as written. It is first-party, from about 2017 (the same page says 'as of February 2017'), gives no command lines or inputs, and disabled threading with -no-threads, which current Options.td no longer has (the equivalent is --threads=1). Its GNU ld rows also drop -icf=all and -gdb-index, which GNU ld did not support.

Harness note on Wild's mold-gdb-index row (12.1x over GNU ld): the runner aborts on any linker error or on output containing 'warning:', and lld's docs say GNU ld lacks --gdb-index. So GNU ld cannot have been given an unsupported --gdb-index. Either its unpublished per-linker flags dropped the option, or GNU ld built no index and did less work than lld. Either way the inputs are unpublished. If GNU ld skipped the index, the ratio understates lld's advantage rather than favouring lld, as the record's caveat suggests.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick lld over mold or wild when you need something they lack: PE/COFF with PDB, Mach-O or WebAssembly output, built-in LTO, an embeddable library, or a linker that rustc and Clang toolchains already ship. Pick mold or wild for raw ELF link speed, where both are several times faster on large debug links. On Mach-O, zld competes only with Apple's ld64; lld's Mach-O port claims more than 2x over ld64, but no numbers were read for that.
verified_claims_summary: Independent benchmark (Wild project, AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX 16C/32T, 92 GiB RAM, output on tmpfs, Ubuntu packages GNU ld 2.46 and LLD 21.1.8, ten batches of eight runs per linker): lld linked ripgrep in about 92 ms vs 451 ms for GNU ld, wild-debug in 215 ms vs 1512 ms and mold-gdb-index in 790 ms vs 9.7 s, with near parity on c-hello-world (19.6 vs 20.7 ms) and LTO (11.4 vs 12.8 s). The ratios are derived from the chart labels; there are no gold rows. The lld docs' own roughly 2017 table, on a 2-socket 20-core Xeon E5-2680, shows threaded lld 2.9x to 4.4x faster than threaded gold and 4.9x to 19.7x faster than GNU ld on ffmpeg, mysqld, clang and chromium debug links.
status_note: Very active: the lld directory had commits from October 2 to October 6, 2026. Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, already packaged by every major distro, and the default linker for rustc on x86-64 Linux, so it is usable today. Three caveats on the evidence: Wild's chart inputs and per-linker flags are unpublished, the docs table is first-party and about nine years old, and lld's speed edge over GNU linkers is now well behind mold and wild on ELF.
